> Graphic design, social media management and Meta ads for Nepali businesses, by Vaishali Sharma in Biratnagar. Hire one person for posts, page handling and ads.

## Social Media Marketing & Graphic Design Services in Nepal

I am Vaishali Sharma, a freelance graphic designer and social media marketer based in Biratnagar. I help Nepali businesses look professional online, stay active on Facebook and Instagram, and turn ad spend into messages and customers.

### Graphic Design

Posts, stories, festival greetings, product posters, logos, menus and brand kits in Canva, Adobe Illustrator and Figma.

Monthly page handling for Facebook and Instagram: planning, design, reels, captions, posting and replies.

- Content calendar with festival dates
- Reels, video editing and AI-assisted video
- Script and caption writing
- Comment and inbox replies

### Meta Ads & Facebook Boosting

Facebook and Instagram ads set up for messages, leads or traffic, with targeting that fits your city and customers.

- Boosting vs Ads Manager, chosen per goal
- Local audience targeting
- Lead replies and follow-up
- Plain-language results report

### Why hire one person for design, content and ads?

A lot of Nepali businesses split their social media between a designer who makes posts, a relative who uploads them, and an agency that boosts them. Each person sees only part of the picture, so the page looks inconsistent, messages go unanswered, and nobody can say which boost actually brought customers.

When the same person designs the post, writes the caption, runs the ad and replies to the people who message, the whole thing fits together. I know which product the ad is pushing because I made the creative, and I know which ads are working because I am the one reading the leads in the inbox.

That is how I work today for Rouniyar International and Bath Nepal (https://vaishalisharma.com.np/portfolio/rouniyar-international-bath-nepal): product posts and reels, festival greetings, scripts, AI-generated video, Meta ads and lead replies, all handled together.

#### Also available: websites and UI design

I hold a BCA from Tribhuvan University and interned as a UI/UX designer at Clove I.T., where I designed six web and mobile interfaces. If your business needs a landing page or a simple website to send ad traffic to, I can design and build that too. See the web projects in my portfolio (https://vaishalisharma.com.np/portfolio/).

#### Areas I serve

In person around Biratnagar and eastern Nepal. Remote everywhere else.

### From first message to monthly report

#### Tell me about your business

Send a message on WhatsApp or the contact form with your page link and what you want more of.

#### Get a plan and quote

I review your page and send a short plan with what I would post, what I would advertise and the monthly cost.

#### Content goes live

You approve the calendar, I design and post, and ads start once the first good posts are up.

#### Review every month

A simple report on reach, messages and leads, and what we change next month.

### Questions about my services

**Q:** Which service should I start with?
If your page is inactive, start with social media management so you have steady content. If your page already posts regularly but brings few enquiries, start with Meta ads. If you only need designs that your own team will post, choose graphic design.

**Q:** Do you offer monthly packages?
Yes. Most clients book a monthly package that combines design, posting, reels and ads. Each package is quoted to your goals rather than taken from a fixed price list.

**Q:** Can you also build a website?
Yes. I trained as a UI/UX designer and front-end developer, and can design and build a landing page or small website for your ads to send people to. See the web projects in my portfolio (https://vaishalisharma.com.np/portfolio/).

**Q:** How quickly can you start?
Usually within a week of agreeing on the plan. Festival campaigns can be prepared sooner if the date is close.

**Q:** How do we communicate?
Mostly on WhatsApp, with a call or an in-person meeting at the start. You approve content through a shared calendar.

## Graphic Designer in Biratnagar, Nepal

I design social media posts, festival greetings, product posters, logos, menus and ad creatives for businesses in Biratnagar and across Nepal. I have more than a year of graphic design experience in Canva, Adobe Illustrator and Figma, and I currently design daily content for Rouniyar International and Bath Nepal.

### Graphic design services

Everything a small or growing business in Nepal needs to look consistent online and in print.

#### Social media post design

Facebook and Instagram posts, carousels and stories designed around your products and brand colors, sized correctly for each placement.

#### Festival and greeting posts

Dashain, Tihar, Chhath, Teej, Holi, Nepali New Year and Vishwakarma Puja greetings with your logo and a proper Nepali message, ready before the day.

#### Logo design and brand kits

A logo that works on a signboard, a Facebook profile picture and a WhatsApp status, plus the colors and fonts to use everywhere else.

Offer posters, product launch flyers, wholesale price lists and flex banners designed to be read in two seconds.

Restaurant, cafe and salon menus that are easy to scan on a phone screen and still look good printed.

Images and short videos made for Meta ads, where the product and the offer have to land before someone scrolls past. See my Meta ads service (https://vaishalisharma.com.np/services/meta-ads).

### How I approach design for Nepali businesses

Most of the people who see your posts are on a phone, scrolling fast, often on mobile data. So I design for that: big readable text, one clear message per post, product photos that are sharp, and file sizes that load quickly.

I also design with the Nepali calendar in mind. A lot of engagement for local businesses comes around festivals, and a greeting that goes up late or looks like a generic template does little for your brand. I plan those posts ahead so they are ready and consistent with the rest of your page.

Language matters too. Many of my posts mix Nepali and English, because that is how customers in Biratnagar and Kathmandu actually read and write. I write or check the Nepali text myself so the message is correct, not just translated.

#### Tools I use

Canva for fast social content, Adobe Illustrator for logos and print work, Figma for layouts and web graphics, and CapCut plus AI video tools for reels and motion posts. I have also created 3D product visuals, such as a 3D smoothie collection, and brand-style social posts like a Nike Instagram concept.

#### What you get

- Source files or editable Canva links, so you are never locked in
- Exports sized for Facebook, Instagram, stories, WhatsApp status and print
- Revisions until the design is right for your brief
- A consistent look across every post, not one-off designs

Also see: social media management (https://vaishalisharma.com.np/services/social-media-management) if you want me to post the designs for you.

### Why consistency beats going viral

Most small business pages in Nepal post in bursts: five posts in one week, then nothing for a month. The algorithm and your customers both notice. A page that posts steadily, answers messages quickly and looks the same every time earns trust, and when someone finally needs a pump, a sofa or a haircut, they remember who kept showing up.

That is why my management work is built around a calendar and a routine, not one-off posts.

# Meta Ads & Facebook Boosting in Nepal | Vaishali Sharma

URL: https://vaishalisharma.com.np/services/meta-ads

> Facebook and Instagram ads for Nepali businesses: post boosting, Meta Ads Manager campaigns for messages and leads, local targeting and lead replies.

## Meta Ads & Facebook Boosting in Nepal

I run Facebook and Instagram ads for Nepali businesses, from simple post boosts to full Meta Ads Manager campaigns for messages, leads and website visits. I set the audience, make the ad creative, watch the spend, reply to the leads that come in, and report what the budget actually brought back.

### What my Meta ads service covers

#### Facebook and Instagram boosting

Boosting the right posts with a proper audience instead of the default settings, so the money reaches people who can actually buy.

#### Ads Manager campaigns

Campaigns built in Meta Ads Manager with the right objective: messages, leads, traffic or awareness, depending on what you want.

#### Local audience targeting

Targeting by city, radius, age and interest, for example people within a set distance of Biratnagar or across Kathmandu Valley.

#### Ad creatives and scripts

I design the images and edit the short videos for each ad, and write the copy and hooks in Nepali or English.

#### Lead replies

When ads bring messages, I reply quickly with prices, details and next steps, which is where most sales are won or lost.

#### Plain reports

A short report on spend, reach, messages, leads and cost per result, without jargon, so you know what to do next.

### Facebook boost vs Meta Ads Manager: what is the difference?

The **Boost** button on a Facebook or Instagram post is the quick option. You pick a budget and a rough audience and the post gets shown to more people. It works for simple awareness, but you get limited control over placements, objectives and testing.

**Meta Ads Manager** is the full tool. It lets you choose a campaign objective (such as messages or leads), run more than one ad against each other, control exactly where the ad shows, exclude people who already follow you, and see a proper breakdown of results.

For most Nepali businesses I use both: boosts for quick posts like festival offers, and Ads Manager campaigns for anything where you want measurable messages or leads.

### Ads built for how Nepal buys

Most customers in Nepal do not buy straight from an ad. They send a message first to ask the price, check stock or ask about delivery. That is why I usually set campaigns up to bring messages on Messenger, Instagram or WhatsApp, and why I treat replying to those messages as part of the ad work, not an extra.

For my current client, Rouniyar International, I run Meta ads on their product and wholesale content and reply to the leads those ads bring in. Being the same person who made the post and answers the inbox means I can see which ads bring serious buyers and which only bring likes.

### Paying for ads from Nepal

Meta bills ads in foreign currency, so Nepali businesses usually pay with a card that supports US dollar payments (many Nepali banks issue dollar or dual-currency cards), or through a local agency that pays Meta and bills you in rupees. I can help you set up the payment method on your own ad account, so the account and its history stay yours.

### Your account stays yours

I work through partner access in Meta Business Suite, so you never have to share your Facebook password. You can see every campaign, and you can remove my access at any time.

#### Get an ads quote

Tell me what you sell, where your customers are and what you want from ads. I will suggest a starting budget and send a quote for managing it.

Ads work better with good content behind them. See social media management (https://vaishalisharma.com.np/services/social-media-management).

### From budget to results

#### Goal and budget

We agree on one goal (messages, leads or visits) and a budget you are comfortable testing.

#### Audience and creative

I set the audience, make two or three ad versions and write the copy.

#### Launch and watch

I check results every few days, pause weak ads and move budget to the ones that work.

#### Reply and report

Leads get answered, and you get a short report with cost per result.

### Meta ads and boosting questions

**Q:** What is the difference between boosting and Meta Ads Manager?
Boosting promotes a single post with basic targeting. Meta Ads Manager gives full control over the campaign objective, audience, placements and testing. I use boosts for quick promotions and Ads Manager for campaigns where you want measurable messages or leads.

**Q:** How much should I spend on Facebook ads in Nepal?
Start with a budget you are comfortable testing for two to four weeks, then increase spend on the ads that bring results. I suggest a starting budget based on your product, location and goal.

**Q:** How do I pay for Facebook ads from Nepal?
Meta charges in foreign currency, so most businesses use a card that supports US dollar payments or pay through a local agency in rupees. I can help you set up payment on your own ad account.

**Q:** Can you target customers in only one city?
Yes. Ads can target a city, a radius around your shop, or a list of towns, for example Biratnagar and Itahari, or specific parts of Kathmandu Valley.

**Q:** Will you reply to the leads from ads?
Yes. Replying to leads is part of how I run ads, because most Nepali customers send a message about price and stock before they buy.

**Q:** Do I need to give you my password?
No. I work through partner access in Meta Business Suite, and you can remove it at any time.

Biratnagar is one of Nepal's biggest trading and industrial cities, and a lot of its businesses are distributors, wholesalers, manufacturers and family-run shops that sell across Koshi Province and beyond. # Rouniyar International & Bath Nepal: Social Media Case Study

URL: https://vaishalisharma.com.np/portfolio/rouniyar-international-bath-nepal

> How Vaishali Sharma runs content, reels, AI video, Meta ads and lead replies for Rouniyar International, a water pump distributor, and Bath Nepal.

## Rouniyar International & Bath Nepal: Social Media Case Study

How I run content, reels, Meta ads and lead replies for a water pump distributor and its bathroom products brand, as the one person behind both accounts.

- Client: Rouniyar International & Bath Nepal
- Role: Content, design, video, ads, lead replies
- Platforms: Instagram, Facebook, Meta Ads
- Timeline: 2026, ongoing

### The client

Rouniyar International (https://www.instagram.com/rouniyarinternational/) is the authorized importer and distributor of Dual Copper and Discover brand water pump motors in Nepal. It sells to retail customers and to dealers who buy wholesale. Bath Nepal (https://www.instagram.com/bathnepal/) is the same company's bathroom products brand, with the line "Modern bathroom solutions for tomorrow".

Two brands, one company, two very different audiences: plumbers, farmers, builders and hardware dealers for pumps, and homeowners renovating a bathroom for Bath Nepal.

### The brief

Both accounts needed to stay active every day, look like two distinct brands instead of one reused template, reach buyers through ads, and turn the people who message into actual enquiries. All of it had to be handled by one person.

### What I do

- **Content planning:** a calendar that mixes product posts, wholesale offers, trend reels and Nepali festival dates for both brands
- **Graphic design:** product posts and festival greetings for Teej and Vishwakarma Puja, each designed in its own brand style ("Powering your business" for Rouniyar, "Build better baths together" for Bath Nepal)
- **Video editing and reels:** product demo reels, wholesale promotion videos and trend-based reels edited in CapCut
- **AI video generation:** AI-generated clips when there is no fresh footage, so the feed does not repeat itself
- **Script writing:** hooks, voice-over scripts and captions in Nepali and English
- **Meta ads:** campaigns on the strongest product and wholesale content
- **Lead replies and engagement:** answering messages from ads, replying to comments and keeping enquiries moving

### How the two brands stay different

Rouniyar International's posts lean practical: the pump, the specifications, the wholesale contact, and a strong "Better products, bigger business" message for dealers. Bath Nepal's posts lean aspirational: clean bathrooms, modern fittings and softer colors. Festival greetings go out on the same day for both, but each carries its own design and message.

### Output so far

- Near-daily posting across both accounts, mixing photos, reels and videos
- Festival campaigns published on time, in Nepali, for both brands
- Meta ads running on product and wholesale content, with enquiries answered by me directly

The accounts are public, so the best proof is to scroll through them: @rouniyarinternational (https://www.instagram.com/rouniyarinternational/) and @bathnepal (https://www.instagram.com/bathnepal/).

### What I learned

For a distributor, the ad is only half the job. Most leads arrive as a short message asking for a price or a dealer contact, and a fast, clear reply matters as much as the creative. Handling both the ads and the inbox lets me see which posts bring serious buyers, and I plan the next month's content around those.

If your business needs the same kind of support, see my social media management (https://vaishalisharma.com.np/services/social-media-management) and Meta ads (https://vaishalisharma.com.np/services/meta-ads) services, or get in touch (https://vaishalisharma.com.np/contact).

# Facebook Boost vs Meta Ads Manager for Nepali Businesses

URL: https://vaishalisharma.com.np/blog/facebook-boost-vs-meta-ads-manager-nepal

> Boost post or Meta Ads Manager? A practical comparison for businesses in Nepal: objectives, targeting, cost per message, and when to use each.

## Facebook Boost vs Meta Ads Manager: Which Should Nepali Businesses Use?

**Quick answer:** use the Boost button for quick, simple promotions like a festival offer or a new product post. Use Meta Ads Manager when you want a specific result, such as messages, leads or website visits, because it gives you the right objective, better targeting, testing and proper reports. Most Nepali businesses get the best value by using both.

Almost every business owner in Nepal has pressed the blue "Boost post" button at least once. It is easy, it takes two minutes, and the post suddenly shows "reached 12,000 people". Then the question comes: did that bring a single customer?

I run Facebook and Instagram ads for businesses in Nepal, including a water pump distributor and a bathroom products brand, and this is the question I get most often. Here is the practical difference between boosting and Meta Ads Manager, and when each one makes sense.

### What the Boost button actually does

Boosting takes one existing post from your Facebook page or Instagram account and pays to show it to more people. You choose:

- A goal (usually "more messages", "more profile visits" or "more people reached")
- An audience (people who like your page, people in a location, or a simple custom audience)
- A daily budget and how many days to run

That is about it. It is designed for speed, not control.

#### When boosting is the right choice

- A festival greeting or offer you want seen by more local people this week
- A post that is already doing well organically and you want to push it further
- A small test budget when you are just starting out

### What Meta Ads Manager adds

Meta Ads Manager is the full advertising tool behind Facebook and Instagram. It is more work to set up, but it gives you control over the things that decide whether your money brings customers:

- **Campaign objective:** you tell Meta exactly what you want (awareness, traffic, engagement, leads or sales), and it shows your ad to the people most likely to do that.
- **Several ads at once:** you can run two or three versions of an ad and let the budget move to the one that works.
- **Placements:** choose where the ad shows, such as Facebook feed, Instagram stories or reels.
- **Exclusions:** stop paying to reach people who already follow you or already bought.
- **Lead forms and message ads:** collect names and phone numbers, or start a Messenger, Instagram or WhatsApp chat directly from the ad.
- **Better reports:** see cost per message or cost per lead, not just reach.

#### When Ads Manager is the right choice

- You want enquiries, not just views
- You sell to a specific group, such as dealers, parents or clinic patients
- You spend regularly on ads and need to know what each rupee brings back
- You want to send people to a website or a WhatsApp chat

### Side-by-side comparison

|  | Boost post | Meta Ads Manager |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Setup time | 2 minutes | 15 to 30 minutes |
| Uses an existing post | Yes, only | Yes, or a new ad made just for ads |
| Campaign objectives | A few simple goals | Full list of objectives |
| Testing several ads | No | Yes |
| Placement control | Limited | Full |
| Reporting | Basic | Detailed, cost per result |
| Best for | Quick local promotions | Messages, leads and sales |

### What works best for Nepali businesses

In Nepal, most customers do not buy directly from an ad. They message first: "price kati ho?", "stock cha?", "delivery hunchha?". So for most small businesses the goal that matters is **messages**, not reach.

That changes how I set up ads:

1. **Pick one clear goal.** Usually messages, sometimes leads for bigger-ticket items.
2. **Target where your buyers are.** A city like Biratnagar or a radius around your shop wastes far less money than all of Nepal.
3. **Make the creative for the ad.** Show the product and the offer in the first second. A beautiful festival greeting rarely sells a pump.
4. **Reply fast.** An ad that brings 50 messages is useless if they wait a day for a reply. I treat lead replies as part of the ad work.
5. **Check results every few days.** Pause weak ads and move budget to the ones bringing real enquiries.

### Common mistakes to avoid

- **Boosting to "people who like your page" only.** They already know you. Reach new people in your area.
- **Choosing "reach" when you want customers.** Meta will find the cheapest views, not the most interested buyers.
- **Targeting the whole country for a local shop.** Someone in Pokhara will not travel to your shop in Itahari.
- **Running the same ad for months.** People stop noticing it. Refresh the creative regularly.
- **Judging by likes.** Judge by messages, leads and sales.

### The short version

Boost when you want quick visibility for a simple post. Use Ads Manager when you want measurable enquiries. And whichever you use, make sure someone is answering the messages.

If you would rather hand this to someone, I set up and manage Meta ads and Facebook boosting for Nepali businesses (https://vaishalisharma.com.np/services/meta-ads), including the creative and the lead replies. You can also read how to pay for Facebook ads from Nepal (https://vaishalisharma.com.np/blog/how-to-pay-for-facebook-ads-from-nepal).

# How to Pay for Facebook Ads from Nepal (2026 Guide)

URL: https://vaishalisharma.com.np/blog/how-to-pay-for-facebook-ads-from-nepal

> Why Nepali cards get declined for Facebook ads, and the options that work: dollar cards, local agencies paid in rupees, and keeping the ad account in your name.

## How to Pay for Facebook Ads from Nepal (2026 Guide)

**Quick answer:** Meta bills Facebook and Instagram ads in foreign currency, and normal Nepali debit cards do not work for it. The two common options are a dollar card (a USD prepaid or dual-currency card issued by a Nepali bank) added to your own ad account, or a local ad agency or service that runs ads for you and takes payment in rupees. For a business that advertises regularly, a dollar card on your own account is usually the better long-term choice.

"How do I pay for boosting from Nepal?" is one of the first questions every small business owner asks, and the answer is not obvious. You press Boost, Facebook asks for a card, and your regular bank card gets declined. Here is how payment for Meta ads works from Nepal, and how to pick the right option.

### Why your normal card does not work

Meta charges advertisers in foreign currency. Nepali debit cards issued in rupees are generally not enabled for international online payments, so Facebook declines them. To pay Meta directly, you need a card that is allowed to make payments in US dollars.

### Option 1: A dollar card on your own ad account

Several Nepali banks issue USD prepaid cards or dual-currency cards that can be used for international online payments, including Facebook and Google ads. You load the card with dollars through your bank and add it as the payment method in Meta.

#### How to get one

1. Ask your bank whether it issues a USD prepaid, virtual dollar or dual-currency card, and what documents it needs (usually your citizenship or passport, and sometimes a PAN for business use).
2. Load the card with the amount you plan to spend.
3. In Meta Business Suite or Ads Manager, open **Billing and payments** and add the card as a payment method.

#### Limits to check

Dollar cards in Nepal come with an annual spending limit set under Nepal Rastra Bank rules. For individual cards this has long been a few hundred dollars a year, and the rules have been changing, so **ask your bank for the current limit** before you plan a big campaign. Businesses with larger ad budgets should ask their bank about options for business or IT-related foreign currency payments.

#### Pros and cons

- **Pro:** the ad account, its history and its data stay yours
- **Pro:** you pay Meta's actual price, with no reseller margin
- **Con:** annual limits and bank paperwork
- **Con:** exchange rate and possible bank fees

### Option 2: Pay a local agency or ad service in rupees

Many agencies and online services in Nepal run ads for you and accept payment in NPR through bank transfer or digital wallets. They pay Meta with their own cards and bill you in rupees.

- **Pro:** no dollar card needed, and you pay in rupees
- **Pro:** good for occasional boosts
- **Con:** a service charge is usually added on top of the ad cost
- **Con:** if ads run on the agency's account, the results and audience data sit with them, not you

If you use this route, ask whether ads will run on your ad account or theirs, and ask for a report showing the actual amount spent with Meta.

### Option 3: A card from family abroad

Some people add a relative's foreign card to their ad account and pay the relative back in Nepal. It works, but it is fragile: if the card owner disputes a charge or the card expires, the ad account can be restricted. It is not a setup I recommend for a business that advertises every month.

### Which option should you choose?

| Your situation | Best option |
| --- | --- |
| You boost once in a while | A local service paid in rupees |
| You advertise every month | A dollar card on your own ad account |
| You spend a lot on ads | Talk to your bank about business foreign currency options |
| You hire a freelancer to manage ads | Your own card on your own account, with the freelancer added as a partner |

### Keep the ad account in your name

Whatever you pay with, the most important thing is that the ad account belongs to your business. When I manage ads for clients, I work through **partner access in Meta Business Suite**. The client keeps ownership of the page, the ad account and the payment method, and can see every campaign and remove my access at any time. Nobody needs to share a Facebook password.

### Tips to avoid payment problems

- Keep enough balance on a prepaid card. Failed payments can pause your ads and sometimes restrict the account.
- Set a **spending limit** on the ad account in Billing so a campaign never spends more than you planned.
- Save Meta's receipts every month for your accounts.
- Do not keep adding and removing different cards. Frequent payment changes can trigger Meta's security checks.

Once payment is sorted, the next question is how to spend it well. Read Facebook Boost vs Meta Ads Manager (https://vaishalisharma.com.np/blog/facebook-boost-vs-meta-ads-manager-nepal), or if you want someone to handle it for you, see my Meta ads and Facebook boosting service (https://vaishalisharma.com.np/services/meta-ads).

# Festival Social Media Posts for Nepali Businesses

URL: https://vaishalisharma.com.np/blog/festival-social-media-posts-nepal

> A festival content plan for business pages in Nepal: the yearly calendar from Nepali New Year to Chhath, post ideas, a Dashain and Tihar plan, and mistakes to avoid.

## Festival Social Media Posts for Nepali Businesses: Dashain, Tihar, Chhath and More

**Quick answer:** plan festival posts at least two weeks ahead, design one greeting per festival in your own brand style, write the message in Nepali, and pair the big festivals (Dashain, Tihar, Chhath) with an offer or product post, not just a greeting. Post on the main day, early in the morning, and reply to every comment.

Festivals are the busiest time of the year for social media in Nepal. Everyone is scrolling, everyone is posting greetings, and customers are spending on clothes, gifts, home repairs and food. It is also when most business pages look the same, because they all use the same free template with a logo pasted in the corner.

I design and post festival content for brand accounts every month, including Teej and Vishwakarma Puja campaigns for Rouniyar International and Bath Nepal. Here is how I plan it, and a calendar you can use for your own page.

### Why festival posts matter for business pages

- **Reach:** people engage more with greetings, so your page shows up in more feeds.
- **Trust:** a well-made greeting in good Nepali shows the business is active and cares about its customers.
- **Sales:** Dashain and Tihar are peak buying seasons for many products.

But a greeting on its own rarely brings customers. The pages that benefit most pair the greeting with an offer, a product reminder or a useful message.

### The festival calendar for Nepali business pages

Exact dates change every year with the lunar calendar, so always check the current Nepali calendar before you schedule.

| Festival | Usual timing | Content idea |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nepali New Year | Baisakh 1 (mid-April) | Greeting plus a "new year, new offer" post |
| Buddha Jayanti | Baisakh full moon | A calm, respectful greeting, no hard selling |
| Janai Purnima and Raksha Bandhan | Shrawan or Bhadra full moon | Gift ideas, family-themed posts |
| Teej | Bhadra (August or September) | Greetings for women customers, red and green themes, clothing and beauty offers |
| Vishwakarma Puja | Around 17 September | Essential for workshops, factories, distributors and tool shops |
| Dashain | Ashwin or Kartik | A series: Ghatasthapana, Fulpati, Maha Ashtami, Vijaya Dashami, plus festival offers |
| Tihar | Kartik | Kaag, Kukur and Laxmi Puja posts, Bhai Tika greeting, lights and gifting offers |
| Chhath | A few days after Tihar | Very important in the Terai and eastern Nepal, including Biratnagar |
| Maghe Sankranti | Magh 1 (mid-January) | Warm, food-themed greeting |
| Holi | Fagun full moon (March) | Bright, playful designs and short reels |
| Mother's Day and Father's Day | Mata Tirtha Aunsi, Kushe Aunsi | Emotional, family-focused posts and gift offers |

### How to plan festival content step by step

1. **Mark the dates two to four weeks ahead.** Designers and printers get busy right before Dashain and Tihar.
2. **Decide what each festival is for.** Pure greeting, offer, product reminder, or a mix. Dashain and Tihar usually deserve a small series, not one post.
3. **Design in your brand style.** Use your colors, fonts and product photos so the greeting still looks like your business. When I made Vishwakarma Puja posts for two brands of the same company, each one kept its own look and tagline.
4. **Write the message in proper Nepali.** Check spelling and tone. A mistake in a festival greeting gets noticed.
5. **Make a reel version.** A short animated or video version of the greeting usually reaches more people than a still image.
6. **Schedule for the morning of the main day.** That is when people are scrolling and sharing greetings.
7. **Boost the offer post, not only the greeting.** If you spend on ads during festivals, put the money behind the post that can bring customers. See boosting vs Ads Manager (https://vaishalisharma.com.np/blog/facebook-boost-vs-meta-ads-manager-nepal).
8. **Reply to every comment and message.** Festival engagement is only useful if someone answers.

### Festival post mistakes to avoid

- Using a free template that thousands of other pages will post the same day
- A tiny logo on a generic image, so nobody remembers which business posted it
- Posting a day late
- Spelling mistakes in the Nepali text
- Hard selling on religious days where a simple, respectful greeting fits better
- Forgetting regional festivals like Chhath if your customers are in the Terai

### A simple Dashain and Tihar content plan

- **2 weeks before:** teaser for your festival offer
- **Ghatasthapana:** greeting that opens the Dashain season
- **Mid-Dashain:** offer or product post, boosted locally
- **Vijaya Dashami:** main greeting post and reel
- **Between Dashain and Tihar:** reminder that the offer is ending
- **Laxmi Puja:** Tihar greeting with lights theme
- **Bhai Tika:** family greeting
- **Chhath:** greeting, especially for eastern Nepal and the Terai

If you want festival posts designed in your brand style and scheduled for you, I offer graphic design (https://vaishalisharma.com.np/services/graphic-design) and full social media management (https://vaishalisharma.com.np/services/social-media-management) for businesses in Biratnagar (https://vaishalisharma.com.np/biratnagar), Kathmandu (https://vaishalisharma.com.np/kathmandu) and across Nepal.

# How to Get More Messages from Your Facebook Page in Nepal

URL: https://vaishalisharma.com.np/blog/get-more-messages-facebook-page-nepal

> Eight practical steps to get more customer messages from a Facebook business page in Nepal: page setup, posts that make people ask, message ads and fast replies.

## How to Get More Messages from Your Facebook Page in Nepal

**Quick answer:** to get more messages from your Facebook page, post consistently with clear product and price information, add a "Send message" or WhatsApp button, end every post with a simple call to action, run message ads targeted to your area, and reply within minutes, not hours. Fast replies turn messages into sales more than anything else.

For most businesses in Nepal, Facebook is not about likes. It is about the inbox. A customer sees a post, sends "price?", and the sale happens in chat. So the real goal of your page is simple: more good messages, answered well.

These are the steps I use on the brand accounts I manage, where I handle both the content and the replies to the leads that come in.

### 1. Fix your page basics first

- **Profile picture:** your logo, readable at small size.
- **Cover image:** what you sell and where, for example "Water pumps and motors, wholesale and retail, Biratnagar".
- **Action button:** set it to Send message or WhatsApp, not "Follow".
- **About section:** location, phone, opening hours and delivery areas.
- **Instant reply and FAQs:** set up automatic answers in Meta Business Suite for common questions like location and hours.

### 2. Post what makes people ask

Posts that only say "Happy Friday" do not bring enquiries. Posts that show a product, a benefit and a reason to ask do.

- **Product posts** with a clear photo, key details and "Message us for price"
- **Short reels** showing the product in use
- **Offers** with a deadline
- **Customer questions** turned into posts ("Which pump for a 3-storey house?")
- **Behind the scenes** of your shop or warehouse, which builds trust

### 3. End every post with one clear action

Tell people exactly what to do: "Message us for today's price", "WhatsApp us for dealer rates", "Comment 'info' and we will message you". One action per post works better than three.

### 4. Post consistently

A page that posts three to five times a week, every week, gets more messages than a page that posts ten times one week and then disappears for a month. Plan a simple calendar so you are never wondering what to post today. Include the festivals, which are your easiest high-engagement days. See my festival content plan for Nepali businesses (https://vaishalisharma.com.np/blog/festival-social-media-posts-nepal).

### 5. Run message ads in your area

Organic reach on Facebook is limited, so a small, steady ad budget helps. Set up ads with the goal of **messages**, target the city or radius where your customers are, and use your best-performing product post or reel as the ad. For the difference between boosting and Ads Manager, read Facebook Boost vs Meta Ads Manager (https://vaishalisharma.com.np/blog/facebook-boost-vs-meta-ads-manager-nepal).

### 6. Reply fast, and reply well

This is where most businesses lose customers. Someone messages at 8 pm asking for a price, gets a reply the next afternoon, and has already bought somewhere else.

- Reply within minutes during business hours
- Give the price or a clear range when asked. "Inbox" as a reply to "price?" frustrates people.
- Ask one follow-up question ("Which area are you in?") to keep the chat going
- Share a phone number or WhatsApp for serious buyers
- Use saved replies in Meta Business Suite for common answers

### 7. Answer comments publicly

Every comment you answer shows the next visitor that the business is active. Reply to questions in the comments and invite them to message for details.

### 8. Track what brings messages

Once a month, look at which posts and ads brought the most messages, and which messages turned into sales. Make more of what works. In Meta Business Suite you can see message counts by post and by ad.

### Checklist

- Action button set to Send message or WhatsApp
- Location, hours and contact in the About section
- Three to five posts a week, with a clear call to action
- At least one reel a week
- Message ads targeted to your area
- Replies within minutes, with real answers
- A monthly look at what worked

Doing all of this every day is a lot alongside running a business. If you want someone to handle the posts, ads and replies together, see my social media management service (https://vaishalisharma.com.np/services/social-media-management) or hire me (https://vaishalisharma.com.np/contact) directly.

# HomeLoom: Furniture E-commerce Case Study | Vaishali Sharma

A furniture e-commerce experience built around craft, warmth, and a shop-to-cart flow that doesn't get in the way.

- Role: UI/UX Design
- Category: E-commerce
- Tools: Figma, HTML/CSS
- Year: 2025

HomeLoom started with a simple brief: a furniture brand wanted an online store that felt less like a catalogue and more like walking into a well-lit showroom. The client made pieces meant to last, with solid wood frames and hand-finished joints, but the existing web presence undersold that craft with generic templates and cramped product photography.

The palette leans into warm tan and olive tones pulled directly from the product photography, rather than a generic neutral grey, so the site reads as an extension of the furniture itself rather than a separate skin wrapped around it.

The core of the work was the shop experience: a homepage that leads with lifestyle imagery and best-sellers, an About page that tells the brand's craft story, an All Products page with category and price filters so browsing large catalogues stays manageable, and a cart page with a running subtotal that updates as items are added or removed. # The UI/UX Design Process, Explained Through Real Case Studies

URL: https://vaishalisharma.com.np/blog/ui-ux-design-process-case-study-walkthrough

> A practical walkthrough of the UI/UX design process (discover, wireframe, design, prototype, build) using four real case studies.

## The UI/UX Design Process, Explained Through Real Case Studies

Most people think "UI/UX process" means a stack of deliverables: personas, wireframes, a Figma file with fifty artboards. In practice it's simpler than that, and far less linear. It's a discipline for making decisions in the right order, so you don't design the visual layer before you understand the problem, and you don't code a flow before you've watched someone try to use it.

I've run this process, in one form or another, on every project in my portfolio (https://vaishalisharma.com.np/portfolio/): a furniture storefront, a footwear brand's landing page and sign-in flow, a fashion e-commerce site, and a travel blog. The tools and the visual language change from project to project. The order almost never does: discover, wireframe, design, prototype, build.

### Why process matters more than the tool

It's tempting to judge a designer's process by their software: Figma versus Sketch, this plugin versus that one. None of that is the actual skill. The skill is knowing which questions have to be answered before you're allowed to move to the next stage, and having the discipline to actually answer them instead of skipping ahead to the part that photographs well for a portfolio.

Skip discovery and you get a beautiful interface for the wrong problem. Skip prototyping and you ship a flow nobody tested, and find out it's broken from support tickets instead of a usability session. The five stages below aren't a formality: each one exists because skipping it has a specific, predictable cost.

### Step 1: Discover, research before you open Figma

Every project starts with constraints, not colors. Before I sketch anything, I want answers to three questions: who is this for, what are they trying to do, and what's actually stopping them right now?

For HomeLoom (https://vaishalisharma.com.np/portfolio/homeloom), a furniture e-commerce concept, the starting brief was about craft and material, but the real design problem was friction in the shop-to-cart journey. Furniture shopping is high-consideration; people compare, second-guess, and abandon carts more than almost any other product category. So discovery wasn't just "what should this look like," it was "where does hesitation happen, and how do we design for it instead of against it."

**The discovery phase is where you decide what a project is actually about**, not the brand's stated goal, but the underlying user behavior you're designing around. Get this wrong and every decision downstream inherits the mistake.

### Step 2: Wireframe, structure before style

Wireframes are where I make layout and hierarchy decisions with none of the distraction of color, type, or imagery. This is deliberate. If a wireframe only works because the hero photo is beautiful, the structure underneath it is doing too little of the job.

A wireframe that nobody argues about usually isn't finished; it just hasn't been looked at closely enough yet.

I keep wireframes low-fidelity long enough to test the argument: does this order of information actually answer the user's questions in the order they ask them? For an e-commerce flow like Glam (https://vaishalisharma.com.np/portfolio/glam), that meant deciding early whether the product grid or the editorial lookbook content should lead the homepage: a decision that shapes everything downstream, and one that's much cheaper to get wrong in grayscale boxes than in a finished comp.

### Step 3: High-fidelity design, where the brand shows up

Once the structure holds up under scrutiny, I move into high-fidelity screens with a real content and component system: actual copy, real product photography (or stand-ins close enough to be honest), and a type and color system consistent enough to reuse across every page, not just the hero.

#### Editorial fashion: Glam

Glam (https://vaishalisharma.com.np/portfolio/glam) is a good example of how visual style has to serve shopping behavior, not just a mood board. Fashion e-commerce customers browse the way they'd flip through a lookbook, so the interface leans into a dusty, editorial palette and generous imagery, while keeping the product grid, filters, and cart mechanics conventional enough that nobody has to relearn how to shop.

#### Warmth and material: HomeLoom

HomeLoom (https://vaishalisharma.com.np/portfolio/homeloom) took the opposite emotional register: warm tones, tactile textures, and typography that reads more like a craft brand than a big-box retailer, because the goal was to make a considered, higher-cost purchase feel less transactional and more like a decision worth taking time over.

The lesson that repeats across both projects: high-fidelity design isn't "add the final colors." It's translating a brand's actual sales psychology into layout, type, and imagery decisions that a customer feels before they consciously notice them.

### Step 4: Prototype and test, catching friction before it ships

This is the step that gets skipped most often, and it's the one that pays off the most. Streets to Runways (https://vaishalisharma.com.np/portfolio/streets-to-runways), a footwear brand landing page and sign-in flow, is the clearest example in my portfolio of why it's worth the extra week.

The original sign-in and checkout flow ran five steps: account details, shipping, verification, payment, and confirmation, each on its own screen. It worked. It also lost people along the way. Usability testing on the interactive prototype (watching real users move through it, not just asking what they thought afterward) showed exactly where the drop-off happened: two of those steps were re-collecting information the user had effectively already given, just in a different form.

- Combined shipping and verification into a single step, since both were collecting contact information
- Moved payment method selection earlier, ahead of the final confirmation screen, to remove a late decision point
- Cut the flow from five steps to three without removing a single required field

None of that came from a hunch. It came from watching people hesitate at the same point, twice, in a row, in a recorded session. That's the value of prototyping before build: it's far cheaper to move a form field in a prototype than to refactor a checkout flow after it's already in production and already losing customers.

### Step 5: Build, where design meets code

I hand-code most of my own front-ends, and that changes how I design. When you know you're the one who has to implement a hover state, a breakpoint, or a loading pattern, you stop designing things that only work at the one artboard size you happened to be looking at when you made them.

**The build phase is a second usability test**, this time against real browsers, real fonts loading asynchronously, and real thumbs on real screens, not a static comp. Spacing that looked generous in Figma sometimes needs to shrink on mobile. A carousel that felt smooth in a prototyping tool needs actual momentum scrolling and touch targets that meet a reasonable minimum size, not just a visual approximation of one.

### What ties these projects together

WanderLust Diaries (https://vaishalisharma.com.np/portfolio/wanderlust-diaries), a travel blog concept, is a useful counterexample to the others, because its design brief was almost the opposite of HomeLoom's or Glam's: get out of the way. The process was the same five steps, but the outcome leaned on large-format photography and minimal chrome, because the thing being "sold" was the feeling of a place, not a physical object with a price tag and a comparison table.

That's really the point of having a repeatable process. It doesn't produce the same-looking output every time; it produces the right output every time, because the discovery phase tells you what "right" means before you've spent hours designing toward the wrong goal.

### A quick process checklist

- **Discover:** identify the real behavior you're designing around, not just the stated brief
- **Wireframe:** prove the structure works in grayscale before adding any style
- **Design:** build a real, reusable component system, not a one-off comp
- **Prototype:** test with real users before a line of production code is written
- **Build:** treat implementation as a second, more honest usability test

If you're planning a product, storefront, or landing page and want a process that catches friction before it ships instead of after, I'd like to hear about it. Get in touch (https://vaishalisharma.com.np/contact) and let's talk through what you're building.

# Glassmorphism vs Neumorphism vs Flat Design in 2026

URL: https://vaishalisharma.com.np/blog/glassmorphism-vs-neumorphism-vs-flat-design-2026

> Glassmorphism, neumorphism and flat design compared: what each UI style is, when to use it, and the contrast and legibility trade-offs in 2026.

## Glassmorphism vs. Neumorphism vs. Flat Design: Choosing the Right UI Style in 2026

Every few years, interface design goes through a style debate that's really a usability debate wearing a trend costume. Right now that debate is glassmorphism versus neumorphism versus flat design, three very different answers to the same question: how much visual depth should an interface pretend to have?

The honest answer is that it depends on what you're building, who's using it, and how much contrast you're willing to trade for atmosphere. Here's how the three actually compare, where each one still earns its place in 2026, and where each one gets teams into accessibility trouble.

### What is glassmorphism?

Glassmorphism simulates frosted glass: translucent panels, background blur, soft borders, and layered depth that let background color and shapes show through a surface without fully revealing it. In CSS terms, it's usually a semi-transparent background color combined with backdrop-filter: blur(), a thin light border, and a soft shadow to lift the panel off the page.

It's not a fringe trend anymore. Frosted, translucent panels are the load-bearing visual language of macOS, Windows' Fluent Design, and Apple's visionOS, which is a big part of why glassmorphism has aged better than most other 2020-era UI trends. It reads as "current operating system," not "current design fad."

#### Where glassmorphism works well

- Navigation bars and overlays that need to feel present without fully blocking the content behind them
- Marketing sites and portfolios where a warm, premium feel matters as much as information density
- Dashboards with a small number of floating cards over a rich background

#### Where it struggles

Glass surfaces need contrast to survive against busy or bright backgrounds, and blur is computationally real. Heavy, continuously animated blur on mobile can quietly tank scroll performance and Core Web Vitals if it isn't scoped carefully.

### What is neumorphism?

Neumorphism (soft UI) makes elements look extruded or pressed into the background using two offset shadows (one light, one dark) on a surface that's nearly the same color as its background. Done well, it looks like the interface is molded out of soft plastic or clay.

It had a real moment a few years ago, largely because it photographed beautifully in design-inspiration posts. It's had a much rougher time in production.

#### The core problem: neumorphism erases contrast on purpose

The entire visual trick depends on a button and its background being nearly the same color, distinguished only by shadow direction. That's the opposite of what accessibility guidelines call for. WCAG 2.x requires a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text and UI components at the AA level, and low-vision users, or anyone viewing a washed-out phone screen in direct sunlight, can lose a neumorphic button's edges entirely.

Neumorphism didn't fade because it was ugly. It faded because it made buttons invisible to exactly the users who needed clear edges the most.

That doesn't make it unusable; it makes it a style that needs deliberate exceptions to its own rules. If you use neumorphism, the safest approach is to reserve it for decorative, low-stakes elements, and pair every interactive control with a real border, icon, or label that doesn't depend on shadow alone to read as clickable.

### What is flat design?

Flat design strips away gradients, shadows, and simulated depth almost entirely, relying on solid color, clear typography, and generous whitespace to establish hierarchy. It's the style that made interfaces faster to build, easier to scale across screen sizes, and, done well, easier to make accessible, because nothing is hiding behind a shadow or a blur.

#### Where flat design wins

- Content-heavy products: dashboards, admin tools, documentation, anything read more than admired
- Teams that need a scalable design system across dozens of screens and states
- Situations where load performance and rendering simplicity matter more than atmosphere

Its weakness is the mirror image of neumorphism's: pushed too far, flat design can feel generic or fail to signal what's clickable, since it deliberately removes most of the visual cues (shadow, gradient, dimension) that historically told users "this is a button." The fix mature flat systems use is color and typographic weight doing the job shadows used to do.

### Side-by-side: how the three compare

- **Depth cue:** glassmorphism uses blur and transparency; neumorphism uses dual offset shadows; flat design uses none
- **Contrast risk:** neumorphism is highest-risk by default; glassmorphism is moderate and background-dependent; flat design is lowest-risk when color choices are deliberate
- **Performance cost:** glassmorphism (blur) is heaviest, neumorphism (shadow) is moderate, flat design is lightest
- **Best fit:** glassmorphism for premium or marketing surfaces, flat design for information-dense products, neumorphism as a small decorative accent rather than a full system

### Accessibility: the part most "which style is best" articles skip

Contrast isn't optional polish; it's the baseline that determines whether people can actually use what you built. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines set contrast minimums at 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text and graphical UI components at the AA level, with AAA raising that to 7:1 and 4.5:1 respectively. Any style choice (glass, neumorphic, or flat) has to clear that bar, and it's worth testing with an actual contrast checker against your real background, not the flattest slide in a mood board.

Blur adds a second, less-discussed risk: legibility. Text or icons placed directly on a heavily blurred glass surface can lose edge definition, especially at small sizes or on lower-quality displays. The safer pattern, the one used across most durable glassmorphic systems, is to keep blur on background panels and containers, and keep text on a more solid, higher-contrast layer inside them, rather than directly on the blurred glass itself.

### Can you mix the three styles?

In practice, most production interfaces already do; they just don't advertise it as "hybrid." A flat design system with one or two glassmorphic overlays (a navbar, a modal, a floating action button) is one of the most common patterns in real products, because it isolates the more expensive, more fragile visual effect to a small number of components instead of applying it everywhere.

What doesn't mix well is neumorphism with anything else, precisely because its low-contrast logic depends on a very specific, muted background. Drop a neumorphic card onto a page with strong color or a busy image behind it and the whole effect collapses: there's no light-versus-dark surface for the shadows to read against. If you want a soft, tactile accent without the accessibility baggage, a subtle inset shadow on an otherwise flat, high-contrast component gets you most of the visual warmth without hiding the edges.

### How this site mixes the two

This portfolio is a flat design system first: paper-colored cards, a solid ink border, and a hard offset shadow instead of a soft blurred one, so the interface reads more like a printed poster than a frosted SaaS panel. Glassmorphism only shows up in a couple of deliberately chosen spots, the sticky navigation bar and a few small hero badges, where a blurred, translucent surface earns its cost by staying legible over moving content underneath. That's the "mix" described above in practice: one dominant style doing most of the work, with a second style borrowed only where it solves a real problem.

### So which should you choose in 2026?

If you're building something that needs to feel premium and modern with a small number of floating surfaces, glassmorphism, used carefully, is the safest of the three depth-based styles, largely because major operating systems have already normalized it for users. If you're building something information-dense that has to scale across many screens and states, flat design remains the most reliable and accessible default. Neumorphism, at this point, is best treated as a decorative accent rather than a foundation: useful in small doses, risky as a full system.

Whatever direction fits your product, the decision should start from your users and your content density, not from what's trending on a design-inspiration feed this month.

If you're weighing a redesign and want a second opinion on which visual direction actually fits your product and your users, get in touch (https://vaishalisharma.com.np/contact), or browse recent case studies (https://vaishalisharma.com.np/portfolio/) to see these principles applied.
